'''''The Geometry of the Octonions''''' is a mathematics book on the [[octonion]]s, a system of numbers generalizing the [[complex number]]s and [[quaternion]]s, presenting its material at a level suitable for undergraduate mathematics students. It was written by [[Tevian Dray]] and [[Corinne Manogue]], and published in 2015 by [[World Scientific]]. The Basic Library List Committee of the [[Mathematical Association of America]] has suggested its inclusion in undergraduate mathematics libraries.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Geometry of the Octonions {{!}} Mathematical Association of America |url=https://www.maa.org/press/maa-reviews/the-geometry-of-the-octonions |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240521073147/https://www.maa.org/press/maa-reviews/the-geometry-of-the-octonions |archive-date=2024-05-21 |access-date=2026-07-20 |website=www.maa.org |language=en}}</ref>

==Topics==
The book is subdivided into three parts, with the second part being the most significant.{{r|elduque}} Its contents combine both a survey of past work in this area, and much of its authors' own researches.{{r|brezov}}

The first part explains the [[Cayley–Dickson construction]],{{r|hunacek|brezov}} which constructs the [[complex number]]s from the [[real number]]s, the [[quaternion]]s from the complex numbers, and the octonions from the quaternions. Related algebras are also discussed, including the [[sedenion]]s (a 16-dimensional real algebra formed in the same way by taking one more step past the octonions) and the split real [[Unital algebra|unital]] [[composition algebra]]s (also called Hurwitz algebras).{{r|elduque}} A particular focus here is on interpreting the multiplication operation of these algebras in a geometric way.{{r|knarr}} Reviewer Danail Brezov notes with disappointment that [[Clifford algebra]]s, although very relevant to this material, are not covered.{{r|brezov}}

The second part of the book uses the octonions and the other [[division algebra]]s associated with it to provide concrete descriptions of the [[Lie group]]s of geometric symmetries. These include [[rotation group]]s, [[spin group]]s, [[symplectic group]]s, and the [[exceptional Lie groups]], which the book interprets as octonionic variants of classical Lie groups.{{r|elduque|knarr}}

The third part applies the octonions in geometric constructions including the [[Hopf fibration]] and its generalizations, the [[Cayley plane]], and the [[E8 lattice|E<sub>8</sub> lattice]]. It also connects them to problems in physics involving the four-dimensional [[Dirac equation]], the [[quantum mechanics]] of relativistic [[fermion]]s, [[spinors]], and the formulation of quantum mechanics using [[Jordan algebra]]s.{{r|elduque|brezov|knarr}} It also includes material on octonionic [[number theory]],{{r|brezov|knarr}} and concludes with a chapter on the [[Freudenthal magic square]] and related constructions.{{r|elduque}}

==Audience and reception==
Although presented at an undergraduate level, ''The Geometry of the Octonions'' is not a textbook: its material is likely too specialized for an undergraduate course, and it lacks exercises or similar material that would be needed to use it as a textbook.{{r|hunacek}} Readers should be familiar with [[linear algebra]], and some experience with [[Lie group]]s would also be helpful.{{r|elduque}} The later chapters on applications in physics are heavier going, and require familiarity with quantum mechanics.{{r|hunacek}}

The book avoids a proof-heavy formal style of mathematical writing,{{r|elduque}} so much so that reviewer Danail Brezov writes that at points it "seems to lack mathematical rigor".{{r|brezov}}

==Related reading==
Multiple reviewers suggest that this work would make a good introduction to the octonions, as a stepping stone to the more advanced material presented in other works on the same topic.{{r|elduque|brezov|knarr}} Their suggestions include the following:
